extracted.intended_audience: trademark practitioners and attorneys practicing before the USPTO (including U.S. counsel for foreign-domiciled clients)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and disciplinary expectations governing attorneys who represent clients before the USPTO in trademark matters, including signature rules, supervision of non-attorney assistants, and obligations during suspension/probation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark signature rule (37 C.F.R. § 2.193; TMEP § 611.01(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: The person(s) identified as the signatory must personally sign the printed form or personally enter the signatory's electronic signature, either directly on the trademark electronic filing system's form or in the emailed form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A person may not delegate their authority to sign, and no person may sign or enter the name of another; typing the electronic signature of another person is not a valid signature; another person may not use document-signing software to create or generate the electronic signature of the named signatory. Impermissible signatures adversely affect the integrity of the federal trademark registration process. See TMEP § 611.01(c) and citations (In re Zhang; In re Dermahose; In re Cowan).

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of applicable rules and potential disciplinary consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are reasonably expected to know (a) the applicable trademark prosecution rules, (b) the provisions of the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct implicated by such representation, and (c) the potential disciplinary consequences when such provisions are violated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO publishes trademark information pages, the TMEP, and OED FOIA records that practitioners are expected to consult; repeated disciplinary decisions illustrate consequences for failing to follow signature and supervision rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competent representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.101)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall provide competent representation, which includes understanding USPTO trademark signature rules and ensuring filings comply with those rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of failing competence include not understanding signature rules, failing to review trademark applications and other documents prepared by non-attorney assistants prior to filing, authorizing non-attorney assistants to enter the practitioner's signature, and failing to consider readily available guidance about delegating signatory authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must act with reasonable diligence, including ensuring filings comply with USPTO regulations and reviewing documents prepared by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific failures: not ensuring filings comply with regulations; failing to review all trademark documents where the practitioner is attorney of record (applications and Office action responses) drafted by non-attorneys; authorizing non-attorneys to enter the practitioner's signature; submitting declarations without conducting a reasonable inquiry into veracity of averments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to avoid false statements / duty to correct (37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a)(1) and (d))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must not knowingly make a false statement of fact or law to the tribunal and must inform the tribunal of material facts known to the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing trademark documents, including declarations, to be presented to the USPTO knowing they were not signed by the named signatory can constitute making or failing to correct false statements; in ex parte proceedings failure to disclose material facts is prohibited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervision of non-attorney assistants (37 C.F.R. § 11.503(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must take reasonable efforts to ensure that non-attorney assistants' conduct is compatible with the practitioner's professional obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failures include allowing non-attorney assistants to prepare and file trademark applications and Office action responses without the practitioner's review, and authorizing non-attorney assistants to enter the practitioner's signature on filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assisting unauthorized practice of law (37 C.F.R. § 11.505)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must not assist in the unauthorized practice of law by establishing processes that permit non-attorney assistants to perform tasks that amount to unauthorized practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishing a process that at times allowed non-attorney assistants to prepare, sign, and file trademark documents on which the practitioner was identified as attorney of record without the practitioner's review or substantive involvement violates this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging in conduct involving misrepresentation includes allowing filings to be presented that misrepresent the identity of the signer or the veracity of averments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: permitting filings not signed by the named signatory; submitting declarations without reasonable inquiry into the truth of their averments, where such declarations are relied upon by examining attorneys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to integrity of trademark system (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner conduct that undermines the integrity of the trademark registration process is prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enabling non-attorney assistants to file trademark applications or other trademark-related documents without the practitioner's review or to enter the practitioner's signature is specifically cited as prejudicial to the system's integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiduciary responsibilities when commodifying legal services
rubrics_metrics.description: While efficiencies and quality control mechanisms may be good business practices, practitioners must ensure such processes do not supplant fiduciary obligations to clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-volume, commodified production of work using non-practitioner assistants may pose ethical pitfalls; practitioners must give full attention to fiduciary duties when structuring business processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. Counsel Rule and obligations for foreign-domiciled clients (37 C.F.R. § 2.11; TMEP § 601)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a requirement of a U.S. licensed attorney for foreign trademark applicants and registrants; practitioners serving as U.S. counsel must be familiar with the rule and its implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final rule and TMEP guidance are cited; practitioners serving foreign clients are expected to know both representation requirements and related ethical obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notification to clients about improper filings
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners have an obligation to notify clients if filings contained improper signatures and to explain potential adverse consequences to their trademark applications or registrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent notified the USPTO that he had informed clients of improper signatures and potential adverse consequences; such notification is part of fulfilling professional responsibilities under 37 C.F.R. § 11.104.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperation with OED investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are expected to cooperate with Office of Enrollment and Discipline investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cooperation examples include agreeing to interviews and providing timely, candid, non-evasive responses to information requests; cooperation can be a mitigating factor in discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and sanctions for rule violations
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO may impose discipline including suspension, probation, publication of orders, and other restrictions for violations of Rules of Professional Conduct and trademark rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This Final Order imposes five months' suspension, probationary conditions, restrictions on USPTO.gov accounts, mandated CLE and TMEP review for reinstatement, and publication of the Final Order in OED FOIA and the Official Gazette. Prior disciplinary decisions are referenced as precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on USPTO.gov accounts during suspension
rubrics_metrics.description: While suspended, a practitioner is prohibited from applying for, obtaining, activating, sponsoring, verifying, or using USPTO.gov accounts to prepare or file documents unless reinstated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office is authorized to disable or suspend any USPTO.gov accounts; respondent prohibited from obtaining or being added to accounts until reinstatement; respondent must not assist others in using such accounts for filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Client notice and limited recognition on suspension (37 C.F.R. § 11.58 provisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must comply with client-notice obligations under 37 C.F.R. § 11.58; limited recognition for up to 30 days may be granted to conclude pending matters, alongside specified notification procedures for foreign clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent may satisfy notice obligations for foreign-domiciled clients by emailing notices in the client's native language to client email addresses, with specific safeguards if using a referring entity's address, and must file affidavits describing measures taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probationary monitoring and reporting requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: During probation, practitioner must perform bi-weekly searches of the USPTO trademark database for matters naming them as attorney of record and promptly report filings made without their knowledge; quarterly written reports to OED are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bi-weekly searches must be reported quarterly; if unauthorized filings are found, practitioner must inform the USPTO Office of Trademark Examination Policy and provide copies of correspondence. Failure to comply can trigger further discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for reinstatement (CLE and training requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: As a condition of reinstatement, practitioner must complete six hours of CLE on legal ethics, thoroughly review all TMEP provisions (including signature requirements), and complete USPTO Trademark Basics Boot Camp (eight modules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioner must submit a declaration/statements attesting to completion of CLE, TMEP review, and Boot Camp; these are prerequisites to reinstatement under 37 C.F.R. § 11.60.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement process for probation violations
rubrics_metrics.description: If OED Director believes practitioner failed to comply during probation, an Order to Show Cause will be issued, practitioner given 15 days to respond, and OED may request immediate additional suspension (up to 12 months) from the USPTO Director.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OED will send Order to Show Cause to address non-compliance; following response and consideration, OED may deliver materials to the USPTO Director requesting further suspension. Such proceedings do not stay the existing suspension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public disclosure and use of disciplinary record
rubrics_metrics.description: The Final Order will be published in OED's FOIA Reading Room and a materially consistent notice will be published in the Official Gazette; the Office may consider the record in future disciplinary matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The record may be used as an aggravating factor, to rebut representations by the respondent, or in reconsideration requests; publication is part of the sanctioning and notice process.
